3.1 Major Branch - The Refuge of Iron.title: 3.1 Major Branch - The Refuge of Iron

text.content:
You run.

Behind you, Highspire burns beneath a sky stained violet and black. The square has become a battlefield of iron stakes, broken wards, and forces you cannot begin to understand. Balor's voice follows you through the smoke, promising secrets and shadows. Marek Thorne's commands ring out above the chaos, cold and precise, as the Bone Coven closes its iron cage.

You turn your back on both.

Whatever Balor is, whatever Marek knows, neither has earned your trust. You will not surrender yourself to a scarred stranger who speaks a name you never knew, nor allow an order of witches to carry you away like some valuable object in their ledger.

There are people still alive in the village.

That must come first.

You push through a burning lane, coughing as smoke fills your lungs. A roof collapses behind you, scattering sparks across the cobblestones. Someone cries for help from beneath the wreckage of a cart, and you stop long enough to pull a frightened boy free. He cannot be more than seven. His face is streaked with soot, and he clutches a wooden horse so tightly that its painted head digs into his palm.

“Where is your mother?” you ask.

He points blindly towards the smoke.

You cannot find her. You cannot promise to return for her. Instead, you take his hand and lead him towards the northern road, where the buildings thin and the fields open beneath the dark outline of the boundary trees.

Others begin to follow.

An elderly man limps behind you, supported by a woman whose sleeve is torn and bloodied. Two farmers carry a third between them. A girl leads a small, trembling dog on a length of rope. None of you knows how many have escaped, or whether the strange fires will spread beyond the village, but the road towards the outer valley remains passable.

You keep moving.

Whenever someone falters, you urge them onwards. When the group begins to scatter, you gather them together. You have no authority, no weapon worth mentioning, and no plan beyond reaching somewhere with walls strong enough to withstand whatever is coming.

For now, that is enough.

The road climbs towards the eastern ridge. Behind you, the village's unnatural light fades into the smoke, though the occasional violet flash still illuminates the clouds. You hear no pursuit. You do not look back to discover whether the Bone Coven has defeated Balor, whether the Fae has escaped, or whether the square has swallowed them both.

You have chosen the living over the answers.

By dawn, the survivors are exhausted. Some have fallen silent, while others speak continuously, repeating fragments of what they witnessed as though saying the words aloud might make the destruction comprehensible. You hear stories of fire that burned without heat, iron that moved without hands, and a figure emerging from the heart of the village.

You say little.

The strange warmth beneath your skin has not faded. It pulses occasionally, a low, persistent sensation beneath your collarbone. Each time it returns, you remember Balor's glowing eyes and the sound of your True Name.

You press a hand against your chest and keep walking.

The garrison appears beyond the ridge shortly after sunrise.

Highspire Garrison stands on a rocky rise overlooking the eastern roads, its walls built from dark stone reinforced with timber and iron. Four squat towers guard the corners, their battlements bristling with crossbows. Smoke rises from the chimneys within, carrying the smell of coal and cooking fires across the cold morning air.

A military standard hangs above the gate. Its faded emblem shows a black tower beneath a silver crown.

You have never been particularly fond of the garrison. Soldiers visit the village to collect taxes, requisition supplies, and remind everyone that the roads belong to the Crown. But its walls are thick, its gates are reinforced, and its guards have weapons designed to fight things more dangerous than ordinary bandits.

Today, you are grateful for all of it.

A queue of refugees stretches from the gatehouse into the muddy approach road. Soldiers direct people into narrow lines, separating families from carts and ordering everyone to put down their belongings. A wagon piled with confiscated tools stands beside the entrance. Another carries iron stakes secured beneath heavy chains.

The gates groan open just wide enough to admit the next group.

Then they close again.

Inside, the bailey is a sea of mud, flickering torches, and huddled refugees. The air smells of wet horsehair, iron, coal smoke, and too many unwashed bodies crowded together beneath damp canvas. Cavalry horses stamp and snort beside the stables, their breath clouding in the morning chill. Soldiers in grey surcoats patrol the wooden battlements with loaded crossbows, scanning the newcomers for signs of supernatural corruption.

The refugees are processed with brisk, impersonal efficiency.

Names are recorded. Belongings are searched. Wounds are inspected for unusual discolouration. Anyone whose skin glows, whose eyes show strange changes, or whose answers seem inconsistent is taken aside for questioning.

You watch a soldier force an elderly farmer to hold out both hands beneath a lantern. The farmer protests that his fingers are blackened only by soot. The soldier tells him to remain still.

Nobody intervenes.

You begin to understand that the garrison offers safety, but not necessarily kindness.

You help your parents across the muddy bailey towards a temporary medical tent. Your mother leans heavily on your arm, while your father insists he can manage until his knees nearly give way. Inside, a garrison medic examines them with hurried hands before directing them towards a straw pallet. He gives you a thin wool blanket, already fraying at the edges.

“They need rest,” he says. “Keep them warm. If either develops a fever, tell the guards.”

You thank him, though you dislike the way his gaze lingers on your parents' faces, searching for something beyond ordinary exhaustion. You spread the blanket over them and wait until their breathing settles. For a moment, with the canvas sheltering you from the wind and the gate closed against the valley, you allow yourself to believe that they might be safe.

Isleen clings to your cloak as heavy cavalry horses clatter past through the mud. Behind them, war-wagons carry bundles of cold iron stakes, each one secured with thick rope. Your sibling watches the soldiers with wide, frightened eyes.

“Are those for the village?” they whisper.

You look at the stakes, then at the guards watching the refugees.

“I don't know,” you answer.

It is the truth, and you hate how little comfort it offers. You draw your sibling closer and guide them towards a sheltered corner of the bailey, keeping your body between them and the passing soldiers. They have endured enough for one night. Whatever questions the garrison has for you, you will do what you can to keep them from becoming frightened again.

You sit on an overturned supply crate near the edge of the bailey, your hands pressed tightly against your collarbone. The heat beneath your skin refuses to dissipate. It comes in faint waves, each one accompanied by a subtle vibration that seems to answer something far beyond the garrison walls.

You watch the guards search refugees, wondering what they would do if they discovered it.

Would they call it corruption? A sickness? Evidence that you had brought the destruction upon Highspire?

You have no answers, and the soldiers offer no reason to trust them. You lower your hands and force your breathing to slow. For now, you are one more exhausted survivor among hundreds. You intend to remain that way.

You are still watching the gate when a heavy hand falls upon your shoulder.

You turn sharply.

The man standing behind you wears a dark grey officer's coat, fastened high at the throat. A pale scar cuts across his jaw, and his cold grey eyes assess you with the practised attention of someone accustomed to identifying threats before they become dangerous.

“You're from the burning valley,” he says flatly.

It is not a question.

His gaze moves briefly over your soot-stained clothes before settling on your face.

“The Commander wants everyone who saw the violet fire brought directly to the high keep.”

Around you, the soldiers continue their work. Nobody looks surprised. Nobody asks whether you wish to go.

You have escaped the burning village, but the safety of the garrison may come with its own price. The officer's hand remains on your shoulder as he waits for your response.

How do you handle being singled out?

choices.text: Comply quietly, keeping your head low to avoid drawing further attention.
Demand to know why the refugees are being treated like prisoners before moving an inch.
Offer tactical information about the roads in exchange for extra rations for your people.

text.content:
The high keep smells of cold iron, wet stone, and something sharp beneath it all, like the air before a lightning strike.

You are led through three guarded corridors before reaching the Commander’s chamber. Each door bears the same symbol: a white bone enclosed within a black iron circle. The guards carry weapons of dark metal, their blades too dull to reflect the torchlight. Cold iron, you realise. You have heard enough stories to know that it is not merely a weapon against the Fae. It is a declaration of intent.

Commander Vane waits behind a broad desk covered in maps. He is older than you expected, with iron-grey hair, a weathered face, and a thin scar running from his left temple to the corner of his mouth. His uniform is immaculate. He does not offer you a seat.

“Tell me what happened at Highspire.”

You begin with the fire.

You describe the violet flames, the strange hum that shook the foundations of your home, and the moment the village seemed to tear open beneath its own streets. You explain how ordinary work, the sort you had performed countless times without consequence, became entangled with something ancient and terrible.

Vane listens without interrupting. His eyes remain fixed on you, though his fingers occasionally move across the ledger beside him, making brief notes in a cramped, precise hand.

You explain the afternoon you spent tending to Elsie, Mara’s feverish daughter. You remember the unnatural pause in the child’s pulse, the faint smell of old ash, and the hearth embers burning white without giving off a sound. You tell him how the fever returned that evening, and how the fire beneath the cottage seemed to answer something in your presence. You cannot explain why. You only know that the strange events began before the village burned.

You describe the merchant’s chest, the hammer that hummed beneath your hand, and the reflection that moved a heartbeat later than it should have. You recount Tomas’s broken cart axle, the iron pin that briefly glowed white, and the sense that something beneath the village was responding to your work. You had repaired wood and metal for years. You had never before felt either material recognise you.

You tell him about the stag at the forest boundary, its unnatural warmth and the dry ash clinging to its fur. You describe the hoofprints that stopped without explanation, the lantern flame turning blue-white, and the fresh tracks that appeared to follow your own back towards Highspire. The forest had been silent that evening. Looking back, you wonder whether it had been waiting for you.

Vane makes a note.

“And then the Fae appeared.”

The word sounds different in this room. Not a legend whispered beside a winter hearth, but a charge laid before a magistrate.

You describe the scarred figure emerging from the violet fire, the shattered silver rings around his wrists, and the way he looked directly at you while the village burned around him.

“Balor,” Vane says, testing the name as though it tastes unpleasant. “And he called you something.”

You hesitate.

“Annan.”

For the first time, Vane's expression changes. It is slight: a tightening around the eyes, a momentary stillness in his hand. But you see it.

“Your True Name,” he says quietly. “Never spoken to you before. Never spoken by anyone who should have known it.”

He closes the ledger.

“Then Marek Thorne arrived with his Bone Coven Wardens, and both sides claimed authority over you. Is that correct?”

You confirm it.

Vane rises and walks to the narrow window overlooking the refugee camp. From here, the survivors appear small and orderly beneath the watchtowers. Smoke rises from cooking fires. Guards patrol between the tents. Beyond the outer wall, the road north disappears into the dark.

“You must understand something,” he says. “The Coven believes your bloodline is a key. Balor believes you can be persuaded to open whatever it is they have spent centuries sealing away. I believe neither side is interested in your welfare.”

He turns back towards you.

“Until we know what you are capable of, you will remain under observation. You will not leave the garrison without permission. You will not speak privately with anyone bearing a Coven insignia. And if that Fae attempts to contact you, you will report it immediately.”

“And if I refuse?”

“Then I will have to decide whether you are a frightened refugee or a threat to every person sheltering behind these walls.”

The guards escort you back downstairs. No one explains whether you are a witness, a prisoner, or something more dangerous. Your people are waiting in the refugee camp, and the Commander’s questions have only made one thing clear: the destruction of Highspire was not the end of your troubles.

It was the beginning of someone else's interest in you.

How do you spend your first week inside Highspire Garrison to survive?

choices.text: Focus on your family and community in the refugee camp.
Offer your labor to the garrison quartermaster to inspect their cold-iron weapons.
Spend your nights watching the battlements, scouting the garrison's weak points.

text.content:
You decide that Commander Vane can keep his questions, his ledgers, and his cold iron. You have spent enough time being examined like a strange object to understand that the answers he wants will not bring your village back. Whatever the Bone Coven believes you are, whatever Balor saw when he looked into your eyes, none of it changes the immediate truth: people are hungry, children are frightened, and the survivors of Highspire have nowhere else to go.

So you return to the refugee camp.

The lower bailey of Highspire Garrison was never designed to house an entire village. Canvas tents crowd the muddy ground between the stable buildings and the outer wall. Families sleep beneath patched blankets, their belongings piled in damp heaps beside them. Cooking fires smoke in the narrow spaces between shelters, and every morning begins with the same arguments over firewood, clean water, and the few remaining loaves of bread.

It is not comfortable, but it is something you can understand.

You help raise shelters from salvaged timber and canvas, tying knots with numb fingers while the wind threatens to pull the whole structure apart. You carry water, mend torn clothing, and organise the distribution of food before tempers can turn hunger into violence. When a child begins crying for a home that no longer exists, you sit beside them until the tears subside. When an older survivor insists they can manage alone, you find a task that allows them to keep their pride while accepting your help.

The work is exhausting. It is also reassuring.

Each completed shelter is a small refusal to let the destruction of Highspire become the destruction of everyone who lived there. Each shared meal restores something the fire tried to take. You cannot rebuild the village, but you can keep its people from becoming strangers to one another.

Your parents settle into a corner of the camp where the wind is less severe. Their age makes the work harder, though neither is willing to admit it. You catch them trying to help with tasks they should leave to others, and you quietly arrange for neighbours to bring them meals and firewood. In the evenings, you sit together beneath a borrowed blanket, listening to the camp settle around you. They rarely speak of the fire directly. Sometimes, the silence says more than words could.

Isleen stays close enough that you can usually reach out and touch her shoulder. She begins helping with small tasks, carrying kindling and sorting salvaged possessions, but you notice how she watches every passing guard and flinches whenever a cart rattles across the stones. At night, Isleen asks whether the village can be rebuilt. You answer as honestly as you can: not today, perhaps not soon, but the people who made it a home are still here.

You have no family member waiting for you beneath the canvas, no familiar voice asking whether you have eaten. The absence is sharpest at mealtimes, when everyone gathers around shared pots and the spaces between people fill with stories of parents, siblings, and lost homes. You find yourself helping others partly because their needs are real, and partly because work leaves less room for the silence waiting when you are alone.

Your own strange inheritance remains, but it becomes easier to ignore while your hands are occupied. The hum beneath your skin quietens as you carry water or stir a pot. The pressure that gathered in your blood at Highspire Square retreats to a distant, almost forgettable sensation.

Almost.

Occasionally, when you touch the iron frame of a cooking brazier, you feel a faint vibration beneath your fingertips. Sometimes a flame leans towards you despite the wind blowing in the opposite direction. Once, you wake convinced that someone has whispered Annan from the other side of the tent wall.

You tell yourself that exhaustion can make shadows of ordinary things.

The camp has enough genuine troubles without inventing new ones.

As the days pass, you begin to recognise the rhythms of your temporary home. The quartermaster's bell rings at dawn. The stablehands curse at the horses before breakfast. Someone always burns the porridge. An elderly woman in the next tent sings while she repairs clothes, and a group of children have started playing a game involving a stick, a wooden cup, and rules that change whenever someone begins to lose.

For brief stretches, life feels almost ordinary.

At night, the cold settles over the bailey. You gather whatever scraps of wood you can find and coax a small fire to life beside your shelter. The flames are ordinary orange, the smoke thin and grey. You watch them carefully anyway.

Kael finds you there more often than not.

He rarely announces himself. You usually notice him by the scrape of his boots on the stones or the familiar sound of him settling beside you. He brings whatever food he has managed to save, breaks it in half without asking, and passes you the larger piece when he thinks you are not looking.

“You know,” he says one evening, “you could let someone else carry the whole camp on their back for once.”

“You volunteering?”

“Absolutely not. I have seen the state of your organisation.”

You nudge him with your shoulder. He laughs quietly, and for a moment the noise of the garrison fades behind the small warmth between you.

Later, when the fire has dwindled to red coals and the others are asleep, Kael reaches for your hand. His fingers are rough and cold from the day's work. He does not make a joke or offer an excuse. He simply holds on, as though the contact is an answer to a question neither of you has been brave enough to ask.

You turn your hand beneath his and lace your fingers together.

There is no grand declaration. No promise that tomorrow will be kinder. Only his shoulder resting against yours, his thumb moving slowly over your knuckles, and the knowledge that you are still capable of feeling something other than fear.

For a little while, that is enough.

On the seventh night, you are woken by frantic pounding.

The canvas flap of your tent shudders as someone strikes it again and again. You sit upright, heart hammering, and reach instinctively for the nearest object that might serve as a weapon.

“Open up!” a guard hisses from outside. “Quietly. Don't wake the whole camp.”

You pull the flap aside.

Two garrison guards stand in the darkness, their faces pale in the lantern light. One holds a spear; the other has drawn a short blade. Beyond them, the camp is still, its tents hunched beneath the moonless sky.

“Someone crossed the inner picket line,” the first guard whispers. “No alarm. No sentry saw them enter.”

“Then where are they?”

The guard looks past you towards the sleeping quarters behind your tent.

“Outside your family's shelter.”

A voice rises from the dark.

“Annan.”

Your blood turns cold.

The speaker does not shout. The name is spoken with the calm familiarity of someone standing at the door of a house they have visited a hundred times. Yet the sound seems to travel through the ground as much as the air. The coals in your little hearth brighten, and every hair along your arms lifts.

“Annan,” the voice repeats. “Come outside.”

One of the guards raises his spear towards the darkness. The other steps in front of you, though his trembling hand betrays how little confidence he has in the weapon.

No one else in the camp stirs. The silence feels deliberate, as though something has pressed a hand over the entire bailey and is waiting to see what you will do.

Kael appears beside you, his expression suddenly stripped of sleep. His hand finds yours, gripping it hard enough to hurt.

Whatever is outside knows your True Name. It has crossed a guarded perimeter without raising an alarm, and it has come directly to the place where your loved ones sleep.

You can no longer pretend that keeping your head down will make you invisible.

choices.text: Step out alone into the night to confront whatever is calling your name.
Wake your Home LI and quietly slip out the back of the tent to retreat into the safe heart of the camp.

text.content:
Kael starts to speak, but you move before he can make a sound.

You place your hand firmly over his mouth and meet his eyes. For one startled heartbeat, he looks ready to pull away. Then he follows your gaze towards the canvas wall.

A silhouette stands beyond it.

The figure is unnaturally still. Its outline wavers against the thin fabric, stretching and contracting as though the darkness around it cannot decide what shape to take. There is no sound of breathing, no scrape of boots against the stones, no shift of weight. Only the faint pressure in your blood, answering the presence outside.

You point towards the rear of the tent.

Kael understands immediately. Whatever questions he might have asked, whatever impulse might have driven him to confront the stranger, he swallows them. He takes your hand, squeezes once, and follows you into the narrow space behind the bedding.

The rear seam has never been properly repaired. You discovered the loose stitching while helping raise the shelter, and you remember thinking that you ought to mend it before the next heavy rain. Now you work the gap apart with trembling fingers, easing the canvas aside without allowing it to rustle.

Cold air slips across your face.

You climb through first, then turn to help Kael. Behind you, the silhouette remains motionless.

Neither of you looks back.

The refugee quarter lies beneath a thin blanket of mist. Most of the camp is asleep, its inhabitants exhausted by grief, hunger, and the unrelenting demands of rebuilding their lives. Lanterns burn at the corners of the bailey, leaving long stretches of shadow between the tents. Somewhere, a horse shifts in its stall. A child coughs in their sleep.

You move slowly, keeping close to the canvas walls.

Kael walks beside you, one hand resting near your elbow to guide you around the worst of the mud. When you reach the sleeping quarters where your family rests, you wake them with the smallest touches you can manage. No explanations. No questions. Just a finger against your lips and an urgent gesture to follow.

Your parents wake reluctantly, bewildered by the hour. Your father begins to ask what is wrong, but your mother sees your face and silences him. You help them into their outer clothes, supporting them across the uneven ground while Kael carries the blanket they had been using. Neither of them argues when you insist that they come with you.

Isleen wakes at your touch, their eyes widening as they see your expression. They begin to ask questions, but you pull them against you and whisper that you need them to be quiet. They obey, gripping your sleeve so tightly that the fabric twists beneath their fingers. Kael takes their other hand, and together you guide them through the darkness.

There is no family to gather, no sleeping figure to wake. You return to Kael instead, finding him waiting with a blanket and the small bundle of possessions you had managed to salvage from Highspire. He looks as though he wants to ask whether you are certain about this. You take the bundle from him and start walking before he can.

The central grain-barn stands near the oldest section of the garrison, a broad stone building that smells of dust, dry straw, and old timber. Most of its grain has already been distributed among the refugees, leaving a clear space along the inner wall. You settle there beneath rough wool blankets, drawing everyone close enough to share warmth.

Only when the barn door is secured do you allow yourself to breathe properly.

For a long time, you listen.

Every distant footstep makes your shoulders tense. Every gust of wind against the shutters threatens to become the sound of someone speaking your name. You keep your hands folded in your lap, afraid that if you let yourself concentrate on the strange heat beneath your skin, it will answer the thing that came looking for you.

Kael sits close beside you.

“You saw it,” he whispers eventually.

You nod.

“And you don't want to know what it was?”

You look towards the sleeping figures beneath the blankets. Beyond the barn walls, the garrison guards continue their patrols. Somewhere in the darkness, the stranger may still be searching.

“I want them safe,” you answer.

Kael studies you for a moment. Then he shifts closer, allowing your shoulder to rest against his.

“Then we'll keep them safe.”

He does not tell you that everything will be fine. He does not promise that the intruder will never return. He simply remains beside you until the darkness begins to thin and the first grey light creeps beneath the barn doors.

When you finally return to your tent, the silhouette is gone.

There are no footprints in the mud. No broken locks, no torn canvas beyond the seam you opened yourself. The guards report finding nothing unusual, and the officer responsible for the inner picket line insists that no one crossed the perimeter during the night.

You do not mention the voice.

Over the following days, you become very good at not mentioning things.

You mend the tent properly. You help secure a better place in the lower bailey, where the stone walls offer shelter from the wind. You organise meals, repair blankets, and trade labour for the small comforts that make a place feel less temporary. You learn which guards are kind, which quartermasters can be persuaded to spare extra supplies, and which neighbours will sit with your family while you work.

Your world grows smaller, but more manageable.

The Commander does not summon you again immediately. The Bone Coven keeps its distance, occupied by matters you neither understand nor wish to investigate. No Fae appears in the refugee camp during daylight. When the nights grow quiet, you begin to believe that perhaps the stranger has lost interest.

The hum in your blood recedes. You stop watching every flame for signs of unnatural colour. You sleep more deeply, though sometimes you wake with the impression that someone has just stepped away from your bedside.

You tell yourself that survival is not cowardice.

You have lost your village. You have seen what happens when ancient powers collide, and you know that the people you love cannot afford another catastrophe. There is no obligation to chase answers simply because they exist. You can choose the small, ordinary things instead: a dry roof, a shared meal, a familiar hand resting in yours.

For the first time since Highspire burned, the future begins to resemble something you might actually live through.

Whether that peace can last is a question you refuse to ask.

choices.text: Embrace this quiet, ordinary life, prioritizing your family's safety above all else.
Watch the horizon at night, feeling a quiet regret that you let the secret slip away into the dark.

text.content:
The garrison smells of damp stone, woodsmoke, and boiled cabbage. It is not a pleasant place, exactly, but after the burning village, you have learned to be grateful for things that are merely unpleasant.

The walls are thick enough to keep out the wind. The roof does not leak too badly. There is a well in the courtyard, a kitchen that serves hot food twice a day, and a narrow room near the western wall where you and Kael have been allowed to sleep. Someone has even managed to find a mattress that is more straw than lump, which feels like a luxury you would once have laughed at.

You have been here for eleven days.

Eleven days of waking to the clang of the gate being opened and closed. Eleven days of watching soldiers patrol the battlements, their faces drawn tight with exhaustion. Eleven days of hearing rumours pass from one corner of the courtyard to another, each more terrible than the last.

The village is gone. The northern road is closed. People have arrived from the outlying farms with stories of strange lights in the hills and smoke rising from places where no houses stand. Some say the Bone Covens are responsible. Others blame the old kings, the witches, or the gods who were supposed to have died centuries ago.

You have stopped asking which story is true.

Truth has become a luxury, too.

Instead, you concentrate on what you can touch.

The rough wool blanket folded at the foot of your bed. The chipped wooden bowl you have claimed as your own. The little patch of sunlight that appears on the western wall each afternoon. The sound of Kael moving around the room while he prepares for another day of work.

This morning, he is trying to repair the strap on his boot.

“You are making it worse,” you tell him.

He looks up from the leather. “I am improving it.”

“You have tied the knot backwards.”

“That is a matter of opinion.”

“It is a matter of knots.”

Kael examines his work with exaggerated seriousness. Then he pulls the strap loose and starts again.

You sit beside him, your knees almost touching. For a little while, neither of you speaks. Outside, someone is calling for more firewood. A child is crying in the courtyard, and a woman is trying to soothe him. Somewhere above you, a soldier laughs at something another has said.

Ordinary sounds.

You have come to treasure them.

Kael finally sets the boot aside. “There. Perfect.”

“You have not finished.”

“I have finished enough.”

You shake your head, but you cannot quite suppress your smile.

He notices. He always notices.

“There you are,” he says quietly.

Your smile fades a little. “Where?”

“You. I have not seen that expression for days.”

You look down at your hands. There are still faint marks beneath your fingernails that no amount of scrubbing has removed. You have tried not to think about what they might be. Ash, perhaps. Soot. Something left over from the night everything changed.

“I am here,” you say.

“I know.”

He does not press you. That is one of the things you have always loved about Kael, even when you have never quite known what to call the feeling. He can sit beside you in silence without demanding that you fill it. He can recognise when you need company and when you need room to breathe.

He reaches for your hand.

His palm is rough and warm, familiar in a way that makes your throat tighten. You remember those hands scraped and muddy when you were children, reaching down to pull you from the riverbank after you slipped on the stones. You remember them carrying stolen bread through the orchard, passing you the larger half even while insisting that he was not hungry.

You remember a hundred small things that seemed insignificant until the world began to disappear.

“I thought I had lost you,” he says.

You turn towards him.

His gaze is fixed on your joined hands. He speaks as though he has been carrying the words for days, waiting for a moment when they might emerge without breaking something open.

“When the fires reached the square, I couldn't see you. I looked everywhere. I thought—”

He stops.

You tighten your fingers around his.

“But you found me.”

“Eventually.”

“Kael.”

He looks at you then, and the expression in his eyes makes the rest of your words unnecessary.

“I know,” he says. “I know you are here.”

For a moment, the room seems very small. There is only the grey light through the narrow window, the faint smell of smoke caught in Kael's cloak, and the warmth of his thumb moving across your knuckles.

You could tell him that you were frightened, too. You could tell him how many times you have woken in the night convinced that you can still hear the village burning. You could admit that sometimes you feel guilty for surviving when so many others did not.

Instead, you lean your head against his shoulder.

Kael goes still for half a heartbeat. Then he shifts to make himself more comfortable, resting his cheek lightly against your hair.

Neither of you says anything more.

You do not need to.

Later, you help in the garrison kitchens. There are too many mouths to feed and too few hands to do it, so everyone who is able must contribute. You peel roots, carry water, mend torn cloth, and do whatever else is needed. Kael spends most of his days helping repair the damaged gate and reinforce the outer wall. He returns each evening with dust on his face and aching shoulders, usually carrying something he has managed to persuade the cooks to spare.

Today, it is an apple.

He places it on the table as though presenting a royal treasure.

“Found it in the stores,” he announces.

“You stole an apple?”

“Rescued it from neglect.”

“You are going to be imprisoned.”

“Then you will have to visit me.”

You cut the apple into pieces and share it with him. It is bruised on one side, but sweet beneath the skin. You eat slowly, saving the last piece for Kael until he catches you trying to slide it onto his side of the table.

“Don't,” he says.

“You like apples.”

“So do you.”

“I have had enough.”

“You have had two pieces.”

“Three.”

“An outrageous feast.”

He pushes the final piece back towards you. You push it towards him again. Eventually, you divide it in half, and the dispute is settled.

That evening, the garrison holds a small gathering in the courtyard. No one calls it a celebration. There is no music beyond a soldier playing a battered wooden flute, and the food is thin stew served in mismatched bowls. But someone has found a handful of dried berries, and a woman from the southern farms tells a story that makes the children laugh.

You sit beside Kael on a low stone step, sharing a blanket against the cold.

For a while, you allow yourself to imagine that this is simply your life now. Not the life you planned, perhaps, but one that can still be lived. There will be work in the morning. There will be meals to prepare and walls to mend. There will be difficult days and news you would rather not hear. There will be people who need help, and perhaps, eventually, a place to call home again.

You cannot promise yourself anything beyond that.

But Kael's shoulder rests against yours, and his hand finds yours beneath the blanket.

“Do you think we'll have a house again?” you ask.

He considers the question rather than answering too quickly.

“Yes,” he says at last. “Not the same one. Perhaps not in the same place. But somewhere.”

“And if we don't?”

“Then we will find somewhere else.”

“You make it sound simple.”

“No.” He looks across the courtyard, where the firelight catches the faces of people who have lost almost everything. “I think it will be difficult. I think there will be days when we don't know what comes next. I think we will have to start again more than once.”

He turns back to you.

“But we can do that together.”

The words are plain. There is no grand declaration, no promise that the world will be kind or that the future will be safe. Kael has never been good at pretending that difficult things are easy.

Perhaps that is why you believe him.

You rest your head against him once more, and he draws the blanket more closely around your shoulders. Above the garrison walls, the night sky is dark and clouded. Beyond them lie roads you cannot travel and places you are not ready to see again.

For now, you remain where you are.

You have a roof over your head. There is warmth in the hearth. Someone is laughing nearby, and someone else is singing softly to a child. Kael's hand is wrapped around yours, steady and familiar.

The world has become smaller, but it has not become empty.

You cannot save what has been lost. You cannot answer every question or undo the terrible things that brought you here. You can only choose what to do with the life that remains.

Tonight, you choose to stay beside him.

Tonight, that is enough.

choices.text: Continue

text.content:
You cannot bear another moment of waiting.

Kael catches your wrist as you reach for the tent flap. His fingers close around you, warm despite the cold creeping through the canvas.

“Don't,” he whispers.

You look at him. You can see the same fear in his face that you feel tightening your chest, but beneath it lies something else: the quiet understanding that whatever stands outside has come for you, and that you cannot protect the people you love by pretending otherwise.

You squeeze his hand once, then gently pull free.

The small iron kitchen knife you took from the cooking supplies sits hidden inside your sleeve. It is a pathetic weapon against anything that can cross a guarded perimeter without being seen, but it is familiar, solid, and real. For tonight, that will have to be enough.

You push aside the heavy canvas flap.

Freezing mud closes around your bare feet. The air bites at your skin, and the frost glittering along the edges of the tents catches the moonlight. Behind you, Kael remains at the entrance, poised to follow if you call for him.

The refugee quarter is silent.

A lantern burns near the central path. Beyond it, the narrow alley between the tents stretches towards the old well-house, its stone walls silvered by frost. The guards who woke you are nowhere to be seen. You cannot tell whether they have retreated for reinforcements or simply lost sight of whatever they were supposed to be watching.

Then you see the figure.

It stands beside the well-house, half concealed by its shadow. Tall, slender, and wrapped in a torn cloak, it looks almost human until you notice the light leaking through the fabric at its side. Silver radiance drips from a wound beneath its ribs, falling onto the frozen mud like liquid moonlight. Wherever it lands, the frost melts in a thin, smoking circle.

The figure lifts its head.

Even at this distance, you recognise something of the presence that emerged from the violet fire at Highspire Square. The same unnatural stillness. The same sense that the world has been forced to accommodate something that does not belong within it.

Yet this is no towering figure commanding a burning battlefield. Its shoulders sag with exhaustion, and one hand presses desperately against its wound.

“You came,” it whispers.

You tighten your grip on the knife hidden in your sleeve.

“Who are you?”

The stranger takes a step forward, then falters. Silver light spills between its fingers.

“Someone who has very little time left.”

It draws a folded piece of parchment from inside its cloak. The paper is stained grey with ash, its edges singed and brittle. A dark red seal holds it closed.

You know the mark pressed into the wax.

You have seen it before, though never on anything that seemed important. It appears on an old object kept among your family's possessions, a mark dismissed as a decorative flourish or an ancestor's insignia. You have never understood its meaning. You have certainly never seen it on a message carried by a wounded stranger who should not be standing inside a military garrison.

The intruder notices your recognition.

“Your family has carried this mark for generations,” it says. “They told you nothing, of course. They rarely do.”

“Stay where you are.”

The figure obeys, but its gaze shifts towards the tents behind you. Towards the thin canvas walls separating the stranger from your sleeping family and the dozens of refugees who have begun to stir at the sound of your voices.

Its expression changes.

Not into a smile. Something more troubling: a sudden, terrible understanding.

“You brought everyone here,” it murmurs. “You gathered them around you. You made yourself easy to find.”

The words strike harder than they should.

“You're the one who came into a guarded camp.”

“And you are the one whose blood they are hunting.”

The stranger glances towards the garrison walls. Somewhere beyond the tents, a sentry calls out a routine challenge. The sound dies away unanswered.

“They are searching these shelters,” the intruder continues. “The Bone Coven has your description. Your name is in their ledgers. They know that something answered when the seal broke at Highspire. They may not know precisely what you are, but they know enough to look for you among the survivors.”

Your stomach tightens.

“Vane said I would be protected.”

“Vane said you would remain under observation.” The stranger's voice is bitter. “There is a difference.”

It moves closer, slowly enough that you could raise the knife before it reached you. The air around it carries an unnatural heat, sharp with the smell of ozone after lightning. Despite the freezing night, you feel warmth against your face.

The parchment remains extended between you.

“Take the key,” it says.

You stare at the sealed message.

“What key?”

“The one they buried in your bloodline. The one the Coven wants to keep sealed, and the one others will kill to possess.” Its voice falters, and for a moment the silver light beneath its skin dims. “I cannot explain everything here. Not while they are watching. But this parchment will tell you where to begin.”

“And why should I trust you?”

“You shouldn't.”

The answer is so immediate that it unsettles you more than a lie would have.

The stranger looks directly into your eyes. There is desperation there, but no attempt to disguise it.

“You can stay here and pretend you are just a farmer, a healer, a craftsperson, a hunter—whatever ordinary life you believe you can recover. You can keep your head down and hope the guards protect your family. Or you can take this key and learn why the world has begun calling your name.”

Behind you, the tent flap shifts.

Kael is still there. You can feel his presence without looking back, a familiar anchor in a night that seems determined to pull everything familiar apart.

The intruder lowers its voice.

“They will use your soft heart against you. They will threaten the people you shelter because they know you will choose them over yourself. And when the choice comes, they will make certain there is no safe answer.”

For a moment, you think you hear something moving beyond the well-house. A scrape of metal against stone. The intruder hears it too. Its head turns sharply, and the silver wound brightens.

“We have seconds,” it whispers.

The parchment is close enough to touch. The knife is still hidden in your sleeve. Behind you are the people you have spent the last week trying to protect.

Whatever happens next, you cannot pretend that the danger has passed.

What do you do?

choices.text: Accept the parchment and hear their proposal in secret.
Raise your knife and order them off garrison land before you call the guards.

text.content:
The stranger's hand trembles as you finally reach for the parchment.

The moment your fingers close around it, warmth spreads through your palm. Not the comforting warmth of a hearth or a living hand, but something deeper, like a coal buried beneath the skin. The sensation travels up your wrist and settles behind your breastbone, matching the rhythm of your heartbeat so precisely that you cannot tell whether the parchment is responding to you or whether your blood has been waiting for it.

The broken wax seal crumbles beneath your thumb.

Your family's mark remains visible in its centre.

You know that mark. You remember seeing it pressed into the lid of your mother's old wooden chest, tucked beneath folded linen and the few possessions she had inherited from her own mother. When you were younger, you asked what it meant. The answer was always the same: an old family emblem, nothing more.

You had believed her.

Now the symbol seems to shift in the weak lantern light, its familiar lines forming a pattern you cannot quite follow. For one impossible moment, you feel as though you are looking at a door from the wrong side.

“Read it,” the stranger whispers.

You unfold the parchment.

The writing is faded, the ink browned with age, but the letters sharpen as your fingers pass over them. Beneath the first lines, a second layer of script emerges, thin and silver, as though the words have been written in moonlight.

To those who bear the blood of the First Wardens:

The vault was not built to imprison monsters. It was built to contain the remnants of a war that neither mortal nor Fae could survive a second time.

Our ancestors were entrusted with the seals. We were not kings, nor priests, nor conquerors. We were ward-keepers, bound by blood to maintain the boundary between the living world and what lies beneath it.

The key was never a thing of iron.

It was us.

Your fingers tighten around the parchment.

The stranger watches your face, its expression grim with recognition.

“Your ancestors helped seal the vault,” it says. “They gave their blood to bind its locks. Their descendants inherited the same power, though most never knew it. The Coven spent generations hiding the truth, making certain your family remained ignorant of what it carried.”

You look down at the words again.

The memory of Highspire returns in fragments: the strange hum beneath the village, the unnatural light in the fire, the moment the earth seemed to open beneath your feet. You had thought your ordinary work had somehow caused a catastrophe. Now you begin to understand that your work may only have awakened something that was already inside you.

“What did I release?”

The stranger's jaw tightens.

“Not everything. Not yet.”

The distinction offers little comfort.

It explains that the vault beneath the old boundary was protected by several interlocking wards. Each depended upon a different combination of blood, iron, and ancient magic. When the seal broke at Highspire, the remaining wards did not all collapse. Instead, the balance shifted. Something on the other side had felt the opening, and something else had noticed that the key was alive.

“You mean Balor.”

At the name, the stranger's eyes brighten.

“Balor is one of those who survived the binding. He is not the whole of what lies beyond the vault, and he is not the only one who wants it opened. Some of the imprisoned would rather remain sealed than see what their freedom would cost. Others would burn the mortal world to escape.”

“And the Bone Coven?”

“They call themselves guardians. Perhaps some of them believe it. But they have used your bloodline as a tool for centuries, and they will not allow you to make your own decision if they can prevent it.”

A distant metallic clang interrupts the conversation.

The stranger turns towards the end of the alley. Torchlight moves between the tents, throwing long shadows across the frost. Boots strike the stones in a steady rhythm.

The patrol is coming closer.

“You have less than an hour,” the stranger says. “Commander Vane's men are preparing to search the refugee quarter for anyone showing signs of blood-corruption. They will examine your hands, your eyes, perhaps even your blood. If they discover what you are, you will not return to your family as a free person.”

The parchment grows warmer.

At the bottom of the page, beneath the ancestral declaration, a final passage appears.

When the ward-keeper's blood answers the broken seal, the first gate will call before the third dawn. The bearer must choose whether to restore the binding, claim the power within, or surrender the key to another.

Three days.

You have no idea what the first gate is, where it lies, or what will happen when it calls. But the words feel less like a prediction than a deadline already in motion.

“What happens if I do nothing?”

The stranger looks towards the tents.

“Then other people will decide for you.”

A horn sounds somewhere above the bailey. Not the alarm for an attack, but a short, sharp signal that sends the garrison into motion. The torches are almost upon you now. You hear a guard call for the refugee quarter to be cleared, followed by the scrape of a gate being opened.

The stranger reaches for your hand.

Its skin is feverishly warm, and silver light pulses beneath it. Up close, you can see how badly wounded it is. Whatever magic sustains it is failing, and the effort of remaining in the mortal world seems to cost it more with every passing moment.

“I cannot make the choice for you,” it says. “But I can show you a way out. I can take you somewhere the Coven cannot easily follow.”

You think of Kael, of your family, of the people sleeping beneath patched canvas who have already lost everything once. You think of Commander Vane's cold eyes and the way his expression changed when he heard your True Name. You think of the village burning violet beneath a sky that seemed to split open.

The parchment rests against your palm like a second heartbeat.

You can hide it and stay. You can investigate the garrison's own secrets. You can flee with the stranger into the wild, or place the parchment in the hands of the very people who may have concealed its truth.

The approaching boots leave little time for indecision.

What do you do with the ultimatum?

choices.text: Conceal the parchment, stay in the tents, and use the knowledge to protect your family and refugees.
Take the parchment down into the armory vaults to see if it matches Highspire's cold-iron seals.
Take the intruder's hand and use the parchment's secret mark to slip through the walls into the wild.
Send the parchment to the Bone Coven at the gates, offering your cooperation in exchange for sanctuary.

text.content:
“Get off our land.”

The words leave your mouth before fear can soften them. You pull the iron knife from your sleeve and raise it between you and the stranger. Your bare feet sink into the freezing mud, but you barely feel the cold now. All you can see is the silver light leaking from the intruder's wound and the parchment you refused to take.

“Leave the refugees alone,” you snarl. “Leave my family alone.”

The figure stares at you.

For one brief moment, something like disbelief crosses its face. Then its eyes flare, the dim silver light within them hardening into a furious, banked glow.

“Fool.”

You draw a deep breath and shout for the guards.

The sound tears through the sleeping quarter. Canvas flaps stir as refugees wake, and a child begins crying somewhere nearby. You shout again, louder this time, demanding that the garrison come at once.

The stranger moves.

It crosses the distance between you with impossible speed, one hand shooting towards your wrist. You twist away and swing the knife, more out of instinct than skill. The blade catches the stranger's forearm, but instead of blood, a stream of silver light spills across the metal.

For a heartbeat, everything stops.

The knife becomes white-hot.

Pain flashes through your fingers as the iron begins to glow, its edges brightening until the weapon looks like a fragment of the sun. A sound like a struck bell rings through the alley. The stranger recoils, and the light beneath its skin surges violently against the cold iron.

The blade shatters.

Fragments scatter across the frozen mud, hissing as they strike the ground. One spinning shard strikes the base of a nearby oil lantern. The glass bursts, and burning oil splashes across a stack of dry canvas and packing straw.

Flame leaps upwards.

You stumble backwards, clutching your scorched hand. The stranger staggers too, its wound blazing with renewed intensity. For the first time, you see genuine fear in its expression.

Not fear of you.

Fear of what the collision has awakened.

“Get away from it!” someone shouts.

A second later, the supply wagon beside the alley catches fire. Flames race up its wooden side and curl beneath the canvas covering. The heat strikes your face, driving you back into the open lane as smoke pours towards the battlements.

Heavy boots thunder across the stones.

“Armed response! Clear the quarter!”

Garrison guards flood the alley from both ends, their armour clattering, their weapons drawn. Crossbows rise in a single, practised movement. Behind them, half-dressed refugees stumble from their tents, shielding their children from the spreading fire.

You raise your hands.

“The stranger attacked me!” you shout. “It came into the camp. I was defending—”

A bolt strikes the ground inches from your foot.

“On your knees!”

You drop instinctively, coughing as smoke thickens around you. A guard seizes your arm and twists it behind your back. Another kicks the shattered knife fragments away from your reach. Someone throws a bucket of sand onto the burning oil, but the flames have already climbed the wagon's side.

Through the smoke, you catch one final glimpse of the intruder.

It stands on the low roof of the well-house, its torn cloak whipping in the heat. Silver light pulses through its body, illuminating the frost beneath its feet. Its gaze finds yours across the chaos.

There is no gratitude in its expression. No apology.

Only a terrible, exhausted anger.

“You have chosen them,” it calls.

Then it steps backwards into the darkness beneath the battlements and vanishes.

A crossbowman fires. The bolt disappears into the shadows without striking anything.

The guards surge towards the well-house, but there is nothing to find. No footprints leading away. No blood on the roof tiles. Only a faint silver smear on the stone, fading even as you watch.

The captain in charge turns on you.

“What was that thing?”

“I don't know.”

“Why was it here?”

“I don't know!”

He grips your shoulder hard enough to make you wince. His eyes flick towards your burned hand, then towards the place where the knife shattered.

“You were holding cold iron when it happened.”

“It attacked me.”

“And now we have a burning supply wagon, frightened refugees, and an unidentified intruder inside a secured military perimeter.”

He looks towards the guards.

“Take them to the Commander.”

Before you can protest, they haul you upright and march you through the smoke. Behind you, the refugees gather in frightened clusters while the garrison fights to contain the flames. You search the crowd for Kael, but the guards force you onwards before you can find him.

Your mind races.

You did what you were supposed to do. You rejected the stranger, defended the camp, and called for the people entrusted with keeping everyone safe. You refused to follow a wounded, possibly dangerous creature into the dark.

Yet the result is a ruined weapon, a burning wagon, and a supernatural intruder who escaped without leaving a trace.

You have proved your willingness to stand with the garrison. You have also placed yourself at the centre of a mystery that Commander Vane will not ignore.

The high keep rises above you, its narrow windows glowing in the darkness. Somewhere inside, Vane is likely already receiving a report of the incident. By dawn, he will want answers.

And this time, he will not be content with your account of what happened at Highspire.

The guards pause at the entrance to the high keep while an officer approaches with a fresh set of orders.

You have two options. You can turn the incident into an opportunity by presenting yourself as a loyal defender of the garrison, or you can use the confusion of the fire to escape the guards and return to the relative safety of the refugee quarter.

choices.text: Claim you were defending the refugees from an assassin to win Commander Vane's trust.
Use the chaos of the fire to slip back into your tent unnoticed.

text.content:
The fastest way to survive inside Highspire Garrison, you decide, is to become useful.

Commander Vane has made it clear that you are being watched. The guards know your face, the officers know your name, and somewhere in the high keep a ledger records everything you said about the night Highspire burned. You cannot make them forget you. You can, however, give them a reason to prefer you working for them rather than sitting idle beneath their scrutiny.

The quartermaster is less difficult to persuade than you expected.

He is a square-built man named Harlowe, with thick forearms, a bristling grey beard, and the permanently irritated expression of someone who has spent his life explaining why soldiers cannot simply be issued another sword whenever they lose one. When you offer your labour in exchange for a place in the armory, he studies your hands before asking what you know about tools.

You explain that you understand the properties of metals, the preparation of remedies, and the importance of handling unfamiliar substances carefully. Harlowe looks sceptical until you identify a jar of improperly stored quicksilver and warn him that its contents have begun to separate. He tests your observation, finds you correct, and grudgingly gives you work sorting supplies.

You explain that you have spent years working with tools, materials, and the stubborn imperfections that turn a simple repair into a day's labour. Harlowe gives you a damaged spearhead and asks whether it can be salvaged. You identify the stress fracture almost immediately and explain how the metal should be reinforced. His expression changes. By the end of the morning, he has found you a place beside the forge.

You explain that you know how to maintain equipment, recognise damage, and work efficiently without wasting supplies. Harlowe asks whether you can tell a sound spear shaft from one likely to split during a thrust. You demonstrate with three discarded weapons, identifying the weaknesses in each. He grunts, apparently satisfied, and puts you to work inspecting the racks.

For the first day, the work is simple enough. You sort spearheads, carry bundles of shafts, pump the forge bellows, and help the armourers maintain the weapons that will be issued to the garrison patrols. The heat of the forge is welcome after the cold of the refugee camp, and the regular rhythm of work gives your thoughts somewhere to settle.

Then Harlowe shows you the cold iron.

It is darker than ordinary iron, with a dull, almost lightless surface. The blades and spearheads are stored separately from the other weapons, each rack marked with the white-bone symbol you have seen throughout the keep. Their edges are kept unnaturally clean, and every weapon is checked before it leaves the armory.

“These are not to be handled without gloves unless you have permission,” Harlowe tells you. “And if you see a crack in the metal, you report it. You do not attempt to repair it yourself.”

You ask why.

“Because a cracked blade can fail when a soldier needs it most.”

It is a sensible answer, delivered with the finality of someone who does not intend to offer another.

But the explanation becomes more revealing when you help prepare the weapons for storage. Heavy bolts are coated with quicksilver and a fine grey powder that Harlowe calls bone-dust. The mixture is measured carefully, applied in narrow bands, and sealed beneath a thin protective coating.

You recognise the smell before you understand why.

Ash. Old bone. The same dry, bitter scent that clung to the stag in the northern woods, or drifted from the foundations of Elsie's cottage on the evening her fever returned.

You keep your expression neutral.

The quartermasters speak openly when they believe you are too occupied to listen. They discuss patrols along the old boundary stones, the declining reliability of the garrison wards, and reports of strange lights appearing beyond the northern roads. One officer complains that the cold-iron stores have been depleted faster than anticipated. Another insists that the reserve vaults must remain sealed unless the Commander gives direct permission.

They are not ignorant of what is happening.

They are frightened.

The military has spent generations preparing for the possibility that something might emerge from the old prisons. The soldiers know that cold iron can disrupt certain forms of magic. The quicksilver is intended to interfere with enchantments, while the bone-dust is said to help identify and weaken supernatural bindings. Together, the materials form a methodical system for fighting enemies most people would dismiss as legends.

Fae. Witches. Anything corrupted by the old powers.

And, if the rumours you overhear are true, people whose blood carries the remnants of those powers.

People like you.

The thought settles heavily in your stomach.

You begin to pay closer attention to the armory's layout. You learn which doors require keys, which corridors are watched continuously, and which guards grow careless during the shift change. You notice the narrow staircase leading beneath the keep, where weapons are taken for storage in the subterranean vaults. Every crate entering the lower levels is counted. Every seal is checked.

You do not ask what lies behind the deepest door.

Not yet.

Over the next three days, you earn Harlowe's grudging respect. He trusts you with increasingly delicate tasks, allowing you to inspect damaged spearheads and help catalogue the cold-iron reserves. You learn how the weapons are distributed and how the vaults are secured. You also discover that the quartermasters are receiving urgent instructions from somewhere higher in the chain of command.

The garrison is preparing for something.

On the fourth evening, you carry a rack of newly inspected cold-iron spears down into the subterranean vaults. The air grows colder as you descend, and the smell of forge smoke gives way to damp stone and old metal. Lanterns hang at regular intervals along the walls, illuminating heavy iron chains fixed into the foundations.

You are halfway through restocking the nearest rack when you hear a sound from beyond the deepest vault door.

A slow, deliberate rattle.

The ward-chains scrape against the stone, then fall silent.

You freeze.

A second rattle follows, harder this time. Dust drifts from the ceiling. The lantern nearest the door flickers, its flame briefly turning a pale, sickly white.

Someone is tampering with the wards.

You set the spear rack down as quietly as you can. The nearest weapon is within reach, its cold-iron blade gleaming dully in the lantern light. Behind the crates, a narrow space offers enough cover to watch the door without being seen.

Another metallic shudder travels through the foundations.

Whatever lies beyond the vault door is awake—or someone is trying to wake it.

You have only a few seconds to decide whether to confront the disturbance or discover who is responsible before they notice you.

choices.text: Draw a cold-iron blade from the rack and move toward the vault door.
Hide behind the weapons crates to see who is tampering with the wards.

text.content:
The chains rattle again.

You stand motionless in the subterranean armory, surrounded by racks of cold-iron halberds, spearheads, and heavy bolts prepared with quicksilver and bone-dust. The lanterns cast long, uneven shadows across the stone walls. The air has grown bitterly cold, carrying the sharp smell of copper, damp rock, and something faintly charred.

You listen.

A scrape comes from beyond the deepest vault door, followed by a dull impact that makes dust sift from the ceiling. Whatever is on the other side is moving with difficulty. The iron chains drag across the flagstones, then fall silent.

You consider your options.

If you approach the door, you will be entering an enclosed space with an unknown threat. If you hide, you may discover who has breached the vault without revealing yourself. Either way, you have little time. The garrison's warding system is clearly under strain, and if the guards discover you here when something goes wrong, your presence will require an explanation.

You take a cold-iron blade from the nearest rack, testing its weight before positioning yourself beside the vault door. You keep your breathing steady and your eyes on the hinges. You do not know what is coming, but you intend to meet it with the best weapon available.

You extinguish your lantern and crouch behind a stack of weapon crates. Darkness swallows most of the chamber, leaving only a thin strip of light beneath the door. You keep your hands close to the locking gear mounted on the wall, ready to pull the mechanism if the opportunity presents itself.

The door groans.

Its upper hinge strains first, the sound travelling through the vault like a low, wounded animal's cry. The iron bands shudder. Then the heavy oak swings inward several inches before striking the stone stop with a violent crack.

A figure staggers through the opening.

For one instant, you see only the silver light leaking from its body. Jagged wounds cross its side and shoulder, each one edged with a dark, metallic residue. Its torn clothing clings to skin that seems almost translucent beneath the lantern glow. Silver blood runs between its fingers and drips onto the flagstones, where it hisses against the stone.

The intruder grips a pillar to keep from falling.

You recognise the unnatural presence immediately. It is the same kind of being that appeared in the burning streets of Highspire, the same sort of creature that crossed the refugee quarter and spoke your True Name into the night.

A partially unbound Fae.

Or something wearing the consequences of an encounter with the Bone Coven.

The figure raises its head and sees you.

Its gaze moves from your face to the weapons surrounding you, then settles on the cold-iron blade in your hand—or the locking mechanism beside your hiding place. A faint, humourless smile touches its mouth.

“Look at you,” Balor rasps. “Living like a rat in an armory, holding iron you don't even know how to ignite.”

You tighten your grip.

“Why are you here?”

Balor laughs, but the sound collapses into a sharp breath of pain. It presses a hand against its ribs. Silver light spills between its fingers, illuminating the wounds left by the garrison's ward-stakes.

“Straight to questions. How very mortal.”

“You broke into a military vault.”

“I entered a room full of weapons designed to destroy me.” Its eyes flick towards the cold-iron racks. “Believe me, I am aware of the irony.”

It takes a step farther into the chamber. The chains behind it drag across the threshold, leaving bright scratches on the stone. You notice that several links have been bent out of shape, as though something forced them apart rather than unlocking them.

Balor follows your gaze.

“They have been strengthening the wards,” it says. “Your Commander has been preparing for something long before your village burned. He knows the old bindings are failing. He knows what will happen when the remaining seals begin to break.”

“And what will happen?”

“That depends on who reaches them first.”

The answer is not enough, and Balor seems to know it.

Its eyes settle on you again.

“You have been helping them stock their weapons. Counting their blades. Learning which doors open and which remain locked. Do you think that makes you safe? The iron will not distinguish between the thing it was made to kill and the blood that carries the same ancient power.”

A cold sensation spreads through your chest.

You remember Harlowe's warnings, the white-bone symbols on the racks, and the quartermasters' hushed conversations about blood-corrupted refugees. The military has prepared for the return of supernatural enemies, but it has also prepared to contain anyone who might be connected to them.

You may already be standing inside your own execution chamber.

Balor sways against the pillar. Its strength is failing. Whatever tore through the wards has left it badly injured, and the silver blood pooling beneath its boots continues to glow.

“What are you seeking in the vaults?” you ask.

For the first time, its expression loses some of its amusement.

“Something they stole.”

“From you?”

“From everyone who was imprisoned when the old war ended.”

A distant clang echoes through the passage above. Voices follow, muffled by the stone: guards approaching, perhaps responding to the disturbance in the ward-chains.

Balor hears them too. Its gaze shifts towards the open doorway, calculating the distance and the time remaining.

“If they find me here, they will seal this vault and kill everything inside it,” it says. “You included, if they decide you have been contaminated.”

“You expect me to help you?”

“No.” It looks directly at you. “I expect you to decide whether you would rather die ignorant or risk learning why your blood opens doors that should have remained closed.”

The lantern flame flickers.

Behind the crates, the locking gear waits beneath your hand. At your side, the cold-iron weapons offer a chance to defend yourself, though you cannot be certain what they would do to a creature bleeding silver light. The approaching footsteps are growing louder.

You have seconds to act.

choices.text: Draw a quicksilver-coated blade from the rack and demand to know what they are seeking in the vaults.
Extinguish your lantern and use the vault's locking gear to seal them inside with you.

text.content:
The approaching footsteps echo through the stone passage.

You reach for the long blade resting in the nearest rack and draw it free. The weapon rings against its wooden supports, the sharp metallic note carrying through the vault. A thin layer of quicksilver coats the blade, catching the lantern light in rippling patterns. You have seen the quartermasters prepare these weapons for use against supernatural enemies. You have never expected to point one at a creature standing close enough to touch.

You raise the sword.

“I know what this iron does to your blood.”

Your voice is steadier than your hands. The point rests level with the intruder's chest, directly above the brightest of his wounds.

Balor looks down at the blade.

Then he laughs.

It is a dry, ragged sound, interrupted by a sharp breath as the movement pulls at his injuries. He presses one hand against the stone pillar, but his eyes remain fixed on you. Silver light trickles between his fingers and drips onto the flagstones.

“Do you?” he asks.

He takes a deliberate step forward.

You hold your ground. The blade's point touches the torn fabric over his chest, and you feel the weapon vibrate in your hands.

The reaction is immediate.

The silver light beneath Balor's skin brightens, not with the violent flare you expected, but with a deep, resonant warmth. It travels through the air between you, making the quicksilver coating on the sword shimmer. The liquid metal gathers into tiny, moving beads, crawling along the blade as though responding to an invisible current.

The temperature rises.

You can feel it against your face, a strange heat that has nothing to do with the forge or the lanterns. The hairs on your arms lift. Somewhere beneath your ribs, the familiar hum of your blood answers the vibration.

Balor's expression changes.

His amusement becomes something more intent.

“There it is,” he whispers. “You feel it, don't you?”

You try to draw the blade back, but for one terrible instant it seems to resist your movement. The quicksilver ripples towards the hilt, gathering in a bright line beneath your fingers. You release a fraction of your grip, afraid the metal will burn through your gloves.

“What are you doing?”

“Nothing.” Balor tilts his head. “You are doing it.”

The words make your stomach turn.

He moves closer until the blade presses against his collarbone. A thin line of silver light appears where the quicksilver touches his skin, but he does not recoil. Instead, he watches you with the unsettling patience of someone waiting for a lock to recognise its key.

“Your blood built these vaults,” he says. “Not the walls, not the doors, not the iron chains. Your ancestors helped establish the bindings beneath this keep. They knew how to close the old gates, and they knew what would happen if the seals failed.”

“I have never been here before.”

“You have never needed to be. The blood remembers what the mind does not.”

The chains behind him rattle.

You glance towards the open vault door. The sound of the guards has grown louder, and a lantern beam briefly sweeps across the corridor outside. You have perhaps a minute before someone discovers that the deepest vault has been breached.

Balor follows your gaze.

“Commander Vane will come down here,” he says. “He will see you standing over me with a quicksilver blade in your hands. He will ask why the ward-chains are broken and why the weapons are responding to your blood.”

“I can explain.”

“Can you?”

He speaks without mockery now.

“Can you explain why the seal beneath Highspire broke when you touched it? Can you explain why I knew your True Name? Can you explain why the same power that opens ancient locks is moving through the iron in your hands?”

You have no answer.

Balor lowers his voice.

“When Vane discovers what you are, he will not let you return to the refugee camp. He will not allow you to live an ordinary life while your blood can open the vaults. He will either bind you to the garrison or make certain you can never become a threat.”

You think of Harlowe's warnings, the weapons coated in quicksilver, and the cold efficiency with which the quartermasters prepare for enemies they have never openly named. You had believed that learning the military's methods would make you safer. Now you wonder whether you have been helping them prepare the instruments of your own captivity.

“What do you want?” you ask.

Balor looks down at the floor.

Beneath your feet, something pulses.

It is faint, but unmistakable: a slow vibration rising through the flagstones, matching the rhythm you felt when the quicksilver first began to move. The ancient chains tremble in their brackets. Dust shakes loose from the ceiling and drifts across the lantern light.

Balor's face tightens with urgency.

“The Coven has an anchor beneath this armory. It holds part of the old binding in place, drawing power from the cold iron stored above it. The anchor is failing, and the Wardens are using it to strengthen their control over whatever remains sealed below.”

“And you want me to destroy it?”

“I want you to understand what it is before they use it against you.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No.” His gaze meets yours. “It is a choice.”

He gestures towards the centre of the vault, where the flagstones form a circular pattern around a black iron plate. You had taken it for a reinforcement beneath the weapons racks. Now you notice the thin grooves carved into its surface, the lines converging on a symbol that resembles your family's mark.

The same mark that appeared on the parchment.

The sword grows warmer in your hands.

“You can use your blood to unlock the anchor,” Balor says. “You can refuse, force me out, and return to your Commander as the loyal servant he believes you to be. Or you can try to tear the quicksilver away from the blade before it finishes responding to you.”

He glances at the weapon.

“Though I would not recommend the last.”

A heavy fist strikes the outer door.

“Open up!” a guard calls. “Identify yourself!”

Balor does not look away from you.

“Choose, little key. Once they enter, the choice may no longer be yours.”

The blade trembles. The anchor pulses beneath the floor. Your blood answers both.

choices.text: Use your blood-resonance to unlock the ancient floor-anchor beneath the armory.
Refuse to touch the anchor and force the intruder out at sword-point.
Try to force the volatile quicksilver away with your bare hands, triggering a magical flare.

text.content:
The air in the lowest sub-vault is cold enough to turn your breath into white mist. Torchlight flickers against rough-hewn granite, casting trembling shadows across rusted iron bars and forgotten crates of quicksilver.

Before you stands the central foundation pillar, a massive column supporting the High Keep above. Embedded deep within its surface is an ancient lock-plate of dull, unpolished iron. Its centre bears an interlocking spiral, identical to the symbol stamped into your family’s parchment.

You draw the parchment from your tunic. The broken seal begins to glow with faint violet light, answering the dormant resonance in your blood. As you bring it closer to the plate, warmth spreads through your fingers. For one heartbeat, the spiral on the parchment and the iron seem to become a single, continuous mark.

Your palm aches as you approach the pillar. The dormant heat beneath your collarbone throbs in time with the deep hum vibrating through the bedrock. When you touch the granite, something beneath the stone answers with a slow, deliberate pulse. You do not know how you recognise the symbol, but you know it was made for someone like you.

Thin channels radiate from the lock-plate, disappearing into the floor and climbing towards the ceiling. Beneath the torchlight, you can just make out the metallic glimmer of cold iron running through the keep's foundations.

This is no structural brace. It is part of a binding network.

Balor's warning returns to you. The Bone Coven has built its power around ancient prisons, and the garrison's weapons may serve a purpose far darker than defending the mortal realm. The High Keep might be a fortress, but it might also be a lock.

Footsteps ring out on the iron stairs behind you.

Quartermaster Harlowe descends, holding a heavy crossbow in both hands. His gaze moves from you to the glowing plate. He stops several steps away, studying the symbol with an expression that shifts from suspicion to grim recognition.

“I've worked these armories for twenty years,” he says quietly. “Every quarter-century, the Coven sends inspectors to examine this pillar. They told us it was a structural brace. Something to reinforce the foundations against cave-ins.”

He glances at the iron channels.

“But you don't surround a brace with warding sigils. You don't forbid measurements or clear the entire lower level whenever the inspectors arrive.”

His eyes settle on the spiral.

“It's a cage lock, isn't it?”

Before you can answer, the hum deepens. Violet light travels through one of the channels and gathers inside the lock-plate. The granite groans, releasing a shower of dust. Somewhere above, a bell begins to ring. One strike, then another.

The garrison alarm.
